Dec. 6th En route
Nadi - Suva by
F1j1 Airlines
4 Engined Heron
Dear P & Pi (Parily and Priends)
My last letter was from Korolevu when we expected to make the
thirty minute flight back to Nadi on the same 1fttle Piper Cub which had
taken us to Korolevu but about 11 a.m. the pilot phoned from Suva to report
that his plane was grounded because of mechanical troubla. So we went by
way, (the road was built be U.S. Marines for deployment of troops to repel
a threatened Japanese invasion) through little villages and fields of sugar
cane.
The latter, sugar, makes up about 50% of Fiji earning with gold
mining 20% and copra another 20%. Of course the
. Indian problem is always
present everywhere, especially in the sugar cane felds and around the
large mill at Lautoka.
It was to this port that we drove from Korolevu
to spend Sunday, hight and get ready for our four day cruise starting the
Following morning. Mostly our preparations were taken up with getting rad
of everything except the few items we would need on board because we had a
letter from the Captain stating that space was difficult to find. We got
down to two over-night bags and we really didn't need all that we had in
then.
The Cathay Hotel, very modern, kept our suit cases for us until we
got back.
The Captain, Trevor Withers, was an old New Zealand Air Foree
wing comnander in World War 2 and a great friend of Harold Catty's.
latter persuaded Withers to join him in a Tuna fishing venture which, as
I wrote in a previous letter, did not work out. After the demise of that
53E372
project Withers bought a boat back in 1951 and started running cruises down
to the Yasawa group of islands scattered more or less in a sixty mile line
starting some forty miles west of Viti lovu, the big island with Nadi at
one end and Suva at the other. The Yasawa group was really discovered and
quite well charted by Capt. Bligh when he and 18 others were cast adrift
by the Bounty Mutineers.
Bligh did not land his long boat and was chased
twice by large war canoes full of Cannibals looking for a little white meat.
Our cruise was through largely uncharted seas with many small passageways
through the Coral reefs. Our ship, the "Blue Ingoon"
1s 50 feet long with
two diesel engines which drive it along about 10 to 15 miles an hour. There
are somewhat cramped quarters for four people in a cabin with upper and
Lower berths, forward of that is a gelley, or dining room to you landlubbers,
where two more passengers slept and there is a "flight deck" aft with a
couch on each side where Debby and I slept. The other passengers were an
English couple, an Australlan woman and her son and a couple from Reno,
Nevada.
We left the dock at tautoka at 10 a.m. in perfect weather. The
crew, in addition to Capt, Withers, consisted of four Fijians and an
Indian cook.
We reached the first island called Waya at 2 pom. where we
anchored, had lunch and then went ashore for an old time Fijian ceremonial
reception by the "Dut" (King) and his warriors. The affection of these
simple natives for Capt, Withers 1s constantly in evidence. They built a
"Bure" or grass house for him with aluminum windows (their own have no
windows) and lined with specially woven mats.
BOSSIISI DO

2 -
The welconing ceremony included the preparation and drinking of Yangona,
the native non-intoxteating drink.
Quite a show. Then a spear dance by
singing of 50 years ago.
He spent the rest of the afternoon on the
beautiful beach in front of the Captaine "bure". Debby and I found sone
fairly good shells. The beach and harbor are surrounded by mountains
heavily wooded above a fringe of coconut palms which skirt the shore. The
meat of the coconut, or "Copra"
› 1s the only cash crop of the Yasawas. The
coconuts are gathered by the natives and carried by boat to a central drying
and shipping point.
Tuesday, Dec. 3» We salled early, past a very high mountain with
one side that drops away straight down for perhapa three or four hundred
feet. It is called "Virgins leap" because legend has it that some two :
hundrod years ago some, invaders over-powered and killed all the warriors on
the island.
The wives and daughters having taken refuge on the mountain
top leaped oft the cliff. The natives have pronised to bury Capt. Withers
on that mountain top. We cruised among the islands with a rod out most of
the time. We took turns fishing and I was lucky enough to catch a 35 1b.
yellow fin tuna, quite a battle. We stopped at a number of villages and
beaches including the "Blue Lagoon" a beautiful coral reef,- surrounded
lagoon with thousands of small highly colored fish swiming in and out of
the multi-colored coral in the crystal clear water.
Our final stop on our second day out was at Nacula island where
we anchored at 6 p.m. At this place as the others we went ashore in a
small dinghy usually in two bout loads. After dinner on board the Captain
announced that the people of the island about thirty in all (excluding
children) had Invited us to cone ashore for Tangona and a "Hele" or
celebration. They had bullt a big fire on the beach and in the light of
that fire they passed the Yangona - tastes like soapy water - when the
warrior in full war paint holds the coconut bowl straight out in front of
him you are supposed to clap your hands once, then hold out your boul into
which he poures the Yangona.
You then must drink it all without stopping.
When your cup is dry you toss 1t on the ground and the natives chant in
Fijian "It is dry". You then clap your hands three times and the ceremony,
so far as you are concerned, is over.
served, sitting on the ground, the natives started singing to the accomplament
of two or three ukes and one guitar.
the first place their language, as Hawaiian, is composed of all vowels and
there is no harsh sound, then their voices and the music are both good and
finally they sing the parts to perfection. Of course they just Love any
excuse to have a celebration. In the early daye the Missionarys taught
them that dancing was very wicked. Of course hymn singing was very good.
The natives loved the hymns, that was ok - but they still wanted to dance
3o the missionarys compromised and let them dance the "Taralala" wherein
you stand side by side with your partner putting your arn around her and
she puts her arm around you. Then you start to shuffle to the musio and
break away when it stops.
The moon came out casting long shadows of the
tall coconut palms on the white beach with the water gently lapping the
shore.
JE1 PI00

They said that the Market would be closed today but that there would be a
cruse ship in port and all the shell peddlers would put their wares out
on tables near the dock. So we went down early this morning and Debby was
able to byy a few shells but nothing sensational.
On our arrival Friday afternoon, Penna Gatty, the widow of
Harold Catty, picked us up in her car and
drove us to her house for a
drink before dinner. She is now married to a man named Maurice Scott,
Speaker of the House of Parliament, a Britisher born on the island. Their
house is on a high hill looking over the magnificent harbor of Suva. The
planting around the house 1s typical of Fiji. Golden and pink shower trees,
lots of hybiscus but oddly enough little bougainvilla. It 1s all open to
the weather with a front porch built around a small swimming pool. Penna
seens quite happy and we both liked her new husband.
Tomorrow, Monday, Dec. Ith, we fly back to Nads on PAgI Alrways,
on Fiji Airways but I found that thi
"life" Involved was Harold Gatty's, not minel
On the 10th we fly to New Caledonia for a week later on Dec. 17th
on to Sydney where our address, as I wrote before, will be c/o P. A. A.
Berger House, 82 Elizabeth Street.
We are both well. The weather is hot the way I 11ke 1t but most
of the hotels are air conditioned. No one wears a coat but the Grand Pactrie
in Suva asked that you wear a tie. Next edition from New Caledonia.
As ever,
Harold
